blogs.title: From Travel Ban to Refugee Freeze: How Pacito Extends Trump v. Hawaii’s Deference Under § 1182(f)
blogs.description: This post would analyze the panel’s conclusion that the government is likely to prevail on the challenge to President Trump’s suspension of refugee admissions, and its near-complete reliance on Trump v. Hawaii. It would explore whether Pacito confirms that § 1182(f) now functions as a broadly available presidential power to override statutory immigration frameworks unless Congress has imposed a clear textual limit, and what that means for future Refugee Act challenges.

blogs.title: Stopping Admissions Is One Thing, Abandoning Admitted Refugees Is Another
blogs.description: This post would focus on the order’s central doctrinal split: the President may likely halt new refugee entry, but the government may still have a statutory duty to provide reception and placement services to refugees already admitted. It would examine how the Ninth Circuit separates admission control from post-entry statutory obligations under 8 U.S.C. § 1522, and why that distinction could become a major feature of future immigration litigation.

blogs.title: Authorization or Obligation? The Real Statutory Fight in Judge Lee’s Partial Dissent
blogs.description: This post would dig into the textual dispute over § 1522. Judge Lee reads the provision as merely authorizing refugee-assistance programs, while the panel treats at least some parts of the statute as imposing mandatory duties once appropriations exist. The post would unpack the competing uses of 'authorized,' 'shall,' and 'to the extent of available appropriations,' and situate the disagreement within larger debates over agency defunding, impoundment-like disputes, and when spending statutes are judicially enforceable.

blogs.title: The Emergency Docket Comes to the Court of Appeals: Pacito’s Stay Order as a Shadow Merits Decision
blogs.description: This post would examine the unusual procedural posture of the case: before issuing a merits opinion, the Ninth Circuit entered an interim stay that both blocks the district court’s injunctions and affirmatively orders the government to reinstate cooperative agreements necessary to provide refugee services. It would discuss how the panel used the Nken factors to do substantial merits work at the stay stage, what that says about appellate management of high-stakes public-law litigation, and whether this kind of quasi-merits relief is becoming normalized below the Supreme Court.
